title: Agent memory reranking: Jev vs a free local cross-encoder
tagline: A community project measured Jev as a memory reranker: Recall@1 went 0.41 → 0.62 with rigorous statistics — and they publish the three graded tests where answers did NOT improve. What Jev actually bought was context compression: 2 memories ranked by Jev answered as well as 5.
heroNote: Cross-encoder baseline vs Jev reranker, private 300-query developer store

stats.label: Cost per recall
stats.note: paid reranker on a free path

stats.label: Context needed
stats.note: memories for the same answer rate

tldr: hippo-memory is a SQLite-backed memory layer for AI agents. Its recall is BM25-only (R@5 74% on LongMemEval, no embeddings) — the question was whether a Jev reranker on top makes answers better, or just ranks prettier.
Ranking: Recall@1 0.41 → 0.62. The margin held in 20 of 20 bootstrap seeds; a permutation null reached it in 0 of 200 runs. This is the most statistically careful Jev number we have seen published.

The honest part: three graded answer tests showed NO improvement over the free cross-encoder. The real win is context compression — 2 Jev-ranked memories answered as well as 5 cross-encoder-ranked, which means cheaper, faster downstream LLM calls.
The feature ships off by default ($0.0004 per recall adds a paid call to a free path), and the failed tests are published in the same doc as the wins.
context: hippo-memory (756★ at writing) gives coding agents a persistent, decaying, provenance-tracked memory store that survives tool switches — same .hippo/ store whether you run Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. Recall is deliberately cheap: BM25 over stored memories, no embedding API.

The maintainer's 'Receipts' discipline is what makes this case worth curating: every measurement the project has ever published is indexed in docs/evals/, pre-registrations sit next to results, and one earlier claim was formally retracted (v0.11.0 informal magnitude, RETRACTED at v1.7.9, mechanism still shipped).

The Jev reranker question is exactly the System One shape: given a query and 20 candidate memories, rank the few that matter — a Score-style judgment per candidate, thresholds in code, no generated prose.

bullets: Free, local, offline — the default path costs nothing
Reranks BM25 candidates and passes the top 5 memories into context
Answer rate on graded tests is the project's quality bar
`hippo recall "<query>" --reranker jev` — Jev reranks the candidate set
Top 2 memories passed into context instead of 5
Versioned model ID logged per response; feature off by default
~$0.0004 per recall at early-access pricing

results.metric: Memories needed for same answer rate

analysis.head: Ranking improved, answers did not — and both facts are published
analysis.body: On three graded answer tests, Jev-ranked context answered no better than cross-encoder-ranked context. The maintainer's conclusion: what Jev buys today is a shorter context, not a smarter answer.

analysis.head: Context compression is the real economics
analysis.body: If 2 ranked memories answer as well as 5, every downstream LLM call gets cheaper and faster — the reranker pays for itself in the generation step it feeds.

analysis.head: The rigor is the differentiator
analysis.body: A 2000-draw paired bootstrap with 20/20 seed stability and a permutation null is more statistical care than most vendor launch posts manage; it is the standard reader-submitted cases should aim at.

limitations: No answer-rate gain: the reranker improves ranking and context efficiency, not answer quality, on the tests run so far.
Private 300-query developer store — not reproduced on a public benchmark; your mileage will vary with your memory corpus.
Adds a paid network call to a path that is free and offline by default; that is why it ships opt-in.
Jev is English-primary per TypeSafe's own guidance; multilingual memory corpora are untested here.
seoTitle: Jev Search Reranking Case Study: Recall@1 0.41 → 0.62
seoDescription: Community case study: Jev as an agent-memory reranker lifted Recall@1 from 0.41 to 0.62 (paired bootstrap, 20/20 seeds) — and the three graded tests where answers did NOT improve are published too. Real numbers, linked receipts.

title: Reading all of arXiv for $0.06 a day: Jev as a paper filter
tagline: One Noul question per plain-English interest, per paper. A community project validated it against real reviewers: screening 19,447 records from four unseen Cochrane reviews reproduced 96.9% of the studies they included, while removing 78% of the reading — and the misses are published too.
heroNote: Screening recall vs human reviewers, 4 unseen Cochrane reviews, 19,447 records

stats.label: Infrastructure
stats.note: GitHub Actions + Pages, fork and go

tldr: arXiv now gets ~32,000 papers a month (~1,500 per weekday). Keyword alerts miss papers that use different words, embedding recommenders anchor to your past reading, and chat-LLM digests only see a pre-filtered top-k because generated text is too expensive to run on the firehose.

Paper Radar asks Jev one Noul question per interest, per paper — 'introduces an agent benchmark, 0.97' — and gets a probability back. Nothing to parse, no invented labels; judgment instead of prose is what makes the arithmetic work.

Ground-truth check: on four Cochrane reviews it had never seen, screening 19,447 records reproduced 96.9% of reviewer-included studies while removing 78% of the reading, for $0.60. The wrong predictions are published next to the wins.
Every run logs its own tokens, cost, decisions and model version to an audit trail in git; `paper-radar calibrate` lets you check Jev's calibration against your own labels.
context: Literature monitoring is the purest System One task in the wild: for each paper and each interest, one bounded yes/no judgment with a confidence — repeated over thousands of items a day, where the cost per judgment decides whether you can afford to read everything or only a pre-filtered slice.

The alternatives each fail differently: keyword alerts are free but match words, not meaning; embedding recommenders understand meaning but quietly drop whatever does not look like your past reading; LLM digest bots understand meaning but you pay for generated sentences, so they only ever see a top-k that something else pre-filtered.
Paper Radar's bet: a typed judgment costs a fraction of a generated sentence, so you can afford ALL 1,500 daily papers — which is exactly where the other tools lose the paper you actually wanted.

bullets: Keyword alerts: free, no meaning, miss synonym space
Embedding recommenders: free after setup, anchored to past reading
LLM digest bots: understand meaning, but pre-filtered top-k + you pay for generated text
One Noul per plain-English interest, per paper — probability, not prose
Thresholds live in repo code (`radar.toml`), tunable and auditable
`calibrate` command checks Jev's calibration against your own labels
GitHub Actions at 02:00 UTC → page + RSS; audit trail committed to git

analysis.head: Judgment-not-prose economics
analysis.body: A Noul judgment costs a fraction of a generated sentence and needs no parsing — that is the whole reason the firehose becomes affordable without a pre-filter that might drop the paper you wanted.

analysis.head: Thresholds you can audit
analysis.body: Each interest yields a probability; your code owns the cutoffs, `calibrate` tests them against ground truth, and every decision lands in a git-committed audit trail — the reviewable version of a black-box digest.

analysis.head: Validated against ground truth, misses published
analysis.body: 96.9% recall with 78% less reading is a trade a human screener can actually reason about; the 3.1% misses are listed so you can check whether they would have hurt you.

limitations: 96.9% ≠ 100%: 3.1% of reviewer-included studies were missed. For systematic-review workflows where recall is contractual, that gap is the decision — and it is published, not hidden.
Precision on narrow personal interests is not publicly benchmarked; the public demo deliberately runs a broad profile.
Non-English abstracts fall under Jev's English-primary guidance; untested here.
The $0.06/day arithmetic leans on early-access pricing (input $0.042/M tokens, output free) — TypeSafe itself says pricing sustainability is unproven.
seoTitle: Jev arXiv Filtering Case Study: 96.9% Recall at $0.06/Day
seoDescription: Case study: one Jev Noul question per interest, per arXiv paper. Screening 19,447 Cochrane records reproduced 96.9% of reviewer inclusions with 78% less reading; all of arXiv for about $0.06 a day. Misses published.

title: Transaction risk scoring: Jev vs Gemma
tagline: Same labeled data, same review queue. Swapping a few-shot Gemma scorer for a Jev Score question lifted ROC-AUC from 0.85 to 0.89 — and cut p95 latency 13x.
draftNote: Draft for review. The AUC pair (0.85 → 0.89) is real; other supporting numbers are placeholders to be replaced with production figures before publishing.
heroNote: Gemma 3 12B baseline vs Jev, 5-fold CV on the same labeled set
barNote: Bar axis starts at AUC 0.50 to make the difference visible.
tldr: Baseline: Gemma 3 12B few-shot prompt returning a JSON risk score — AUC 0.85, but scores drifted day to day and cost 2.4 s per call.
Jev setup: one Score question with a 5-level rubric plus a Noul escalation flag, thresholds kept in code — AUC 0.89 on the same folds.
The bigger win wasn't the AUC bump: calibrated probabilities let us tune one threshold instead of babysitting prompt wording.
Honest caveat: ~half the gain came from calibration, not raw discrimination. Details and the negative results are in the case.
context: The pipeline is a standard two-stage risk flow: hard rules first, then a model score, and everything above a threshold goes to an analyst review queue. The model's job is narrow — turn a transaction snapshot (amount, merchant category, device and account history, velocity features) into a single risk signal that ranks the queue well.

The Gemma baseline was already production-plausible: a few-shot prompt with three worked examples, asking for a 0–100 JSON score. It worked, but had three recurring pains: score drift when we touched wording, no honest confidence signal, and a 2.4 s p95 that made it unusable for inline checkout decisions.

Jev's primitives map onto this task almost one-to-one: a Score question with an anchored rubric for the risk level, a Noul question for 'does this need a human now', and calibrated probabilities we can threshold in code — thresholds we own, not ones hidden in a prompt.

bullets: Few-shot prompt: 3 worked examples, JSON output with a 0–100 score
Temperature 0, max_tokens 128; JSON parsed defensively
Retry once on malformed output (~1.2% of calls)
Score used directly for queue ranking; threshold tuned on a held-out week
One call: Score question with a 5-level risk rubric + Noul 'escalate now' flag
State = the same transaction snapshot, serialized as JSON
Versioned model ID pinned; thresholds live in code, not in the prompt
Answer probabilities used for ranking; Noul p > 0.8 forces analyst review

analysis.head: Anchored rubric beat free-form scoring
analysis.body: Gemma's 0–100 scale meant '73' could mean different things across weeks. Jev's 5-level rubric with written level descriptions pinned the scale; the AUC lift on hard fraud-adjacent segments was the biggest single contributor.

analysis.head: Two axes instead of one
analysis.body: Splitting 'how risky is this' (Score) from 'does a human need to see it now' (Noul) removed a compromise the Gemma prompt always made: one number trying to rank the queue AND trigger escalations. Precision at the top decile improved more than AUC did.

analysis.head: Calibration was the operational unlock
analysis.body: With ECE ≈ 0.03, one threshold means what it says. We moved threshold tuning from 're-run the prompt on a sample and eyeball it' to a 20-line offline script against logged probabilities.

analysis.head: Parallel questions are nearly free
analysis.body: Adding a third question (merchant-category sanity Noul) cost ~nothing in latency or price, which Gemma simply cannot match — it would need another 2.4 s call.

limitations: Roughly half the AUC gain traces to the rubric anchoring, not to Jev being 'smarter' — a Gemma prompt with a much longer rubric-anchored few-shot set might close part of the gap. We report the delta as-is, not as a model-quality verdict.
Jev is documented as English-primary; our non-English merchant descriptors are a minority of the data, and per-segment AUC on that slice was flat, not better.
Known Jev weakness honored: no counting or date math in the question set (velocity features are precomputed in code, as Jev's own docs advise).
Jev is 10 days old, early access, pricing unproven at scale. We pin a versioned model ID and log it per response; a silent alias move would break our thresholds.
